(CNN) -- In the pre-dawn darkness Saturday, long after her parents and brother were asleep, Atefeh Yazdi lay in bed cradling the house phone and her cell phone in her hands. Atefeh Yazdi visits with her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, during his trip to America last year. The only light was from a television tuned to the latest news from Iran, and her laptop displaying her Facebook page in hope of any updates on what was happening halfway around the world. "I kind of felt I was more there when I couldn't see the rest of the room, just the TV and the Facebook," the 28-year-old Iranian-American told CNN by telephone from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. Repeated calls to relatives in Tehran only got the "annoying" Farsi-language error message. She recounted the thoughts running through her brain all night: "Are they going to really shoot people? What's going to happen? Is this going to turn into massive killing and violence?" In Houston, Texas, Reza Soltani said the anxiety of waiting and wondering was like endless pacing at a hospital during a loved one's operation. "It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn't ended," Soltani, 28, told CNN by telephone. "I'm worried. I'm hoping it will be good but I'm worried it will get very ugly." The jumble of emotions -- fear, hope, anxiety, frustration -- were reality for millions of Iranian-Americans trying to find out if Iranian authorities would crush protests over last week's election. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the overwhelming victor in voting that opposition groups called rigged. No independent monitors were permitted for the election. A threatening statement Friday by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei increased fears of bloodshed. Iranian authorities have cut off traditional communications such as cell phone connections, and also banned foreign news outlets from covering the protests. Thousands of protesters took to the streets Saturday, even though the demonstrations were banned and police confronted them with clubs, tear gas and water cannons. The uncertainty and unrest strikes close to home for Yazdi, whose grandfather -- a longtime politician in Iran -- was arrested from his hospital bed this week. He's been returned to the hospital, she said, but she doesn't know if he'll be arrested again or what will happen to other relatives. "It's very exhausting," Yazdi said. "I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don't care about the risks involved." Her parents, who left Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, say such talk is foolish, she said. They are as worried as she is, but fear returning now would bring too much risk. "There's a generation gap, a culture gap," she explained. It runs deep, defining her life as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States, who refers to Iranians as "my people." "Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I'm culturally confused," Yazdi said. "I'm not completely American the right way, and I'm not completely Iranian the right way." Soltani also mentioned the generation gap among Iranian-Americans, but he described it as more political. His parents' generation lost everything in the revolution, and will only consider returning when the revolutionary regime has been toppled, he said. Older Iranian-Americans in the United States "actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you're just legitimizing the government," Soltani said. "We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you're going to the other team," is how Soltani characterized their attitude. "They think the system needs to go completely," he said. "All they care is for the system to collapse. They think if the system collapses, they're going to be able to go back." No matter what happens, Soltani and Yazdi said, Iran is changed forever by this week's events. "I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive," Soltani said. "Even if they fail now, the people know if they get in the streets in millions, they're not going to be able to stop them."

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — In the predawn darkness of Saturday morning, long after her parents and brother had fallen asleep, Atefeh Yazdi lay in bed cradling both the house phone and her cell phone in her hands.

Atefeh Yazdi visits with her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, during his trip to America last year.

The only light in the room came from a television tuned to the latest news from Iran and from her laptop, which displayed her Facebook page as she waited for any updates on events unfolding halfway around the world.

“I kind of felt I was more there when I couldn’t see the rest of the room, just the TV and the Facebook,” the 28-year-old Iranian-American told CNN by telephone from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania.

Repeated calls to relatives in Tehran yielded only the “annoying” Farsi-language error message. She described the thoughts that raced through her mind throughout the night: “Are they going to really shoot people? What’s going to happen? Is this going to turn into massive killing and violence?”

In Houston, Texas, Reza Soltani said the anxiety of waiting and wondering felt like endlessly pacing the halls of a hospital while a loved one was in surgery.

“It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn’t ended,” Soltani, 28, told CNN by telephone. “I’m worried. I’m hoping it will be good, but I’m worried it will get very ugly.”

For millions of Iranian-Americans trying to determine whether Iranian authorities would crush protests over last week’s election, the mix of emotions—fear, hope, anxiety and frustration—was all too real.

President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the overwhelming victor in a vote that opposition groups called rigged. No independent monitors were permitted to observe the election.

A threatening statement issued Friday by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei heightened fears of bloodshed. Iranian authorities have cut off traditional communications, including cell phone connections, and have also barred foreign news outlets from covering the protests.

Thousands of demonstrators took to the streets Saturday, despite a ban on the protests, as police confronted them with clubs, tear gas and water cannons.

For Yazdi, the uncertainty and unrest strike close to home. Her grandfather, a longtime politician in Iran, was arrested from his hospital bed this week. He has since been returned to the hospital, she said, but she does not know whether he will be arrested again or what will happen to other relatives.

“It’s very exhausting,” Yazdi said. “I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don’t care about the risks involved.”

Her parents, who left Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, say such talk is foolish, she said. They are as worried as she is, but they fear that returning now would carry too much risk.

“There’s a generation gap, a culture gap,” she explained.

That divide runs deep, shaping her life as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States, and as someone who refers to Iranians as “my people.”

“Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I’m culturally confused,” Yazdi said. “I’m not completely American the right way, and I’m not completely Iranian the right way.”

Soltani also spoke of a generation gap among Iranian-Americans, though he described it as more political in nature. His parents’ generation lost everything in the revolution and will consider returning only when the revolutionary regime has been toppled, he said.

Older Iranian-Americans in the United States “actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you’re just legitimizing the government,” Soltani said.

“We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you’re going to the other team,” is how Soltani characterized their attitude.

“They think the system needs to go completely,” he said. “All they care is for the system to collapse. They think if the system collapses, they’re going to be able to go back.”

Whatever happens, Soltani and Yazdi said, Iran has been changed forever by this week’s events.

“I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive,” Soltani said. “Even if they fail now, the people know if they get in the streets in millions, they’re not going to be able to stop them.”
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Before sunrise on Saturday, while her parents and brother were still sleeping, Atefeh Yazdi remained awake in bed, holding both the family telephone and her mobile phone. During his visit to the United States the previous year, Yazdi had spent time with her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi.

The room was dark except for the glow of a television carrying the latest reports from Iran and the light from her laptop, where her Facebook page was open as she searched for any new information about events unfolding thousands of miles away.

“When I couldn’t see anything else in the room — only the TV and Facebook — I sort of felt closer to being there,” the 28-year-old Iranian-American said in a phone interview with CNN from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania.

Her repeated attempts to reach family members in Tehran led only to what she described as the “annoying” Farsi-language error recording. She said the same questions raced through her mind throughout the night: “Are they really going to shoot people? What’s going to happen? Is this going to become mass killing and violence?”

In Houston, Texas, 28-year-old Reza Soltani described the fear and uncertainty as similar to pacing endlessly in a hospital while someone close to you is undergoing surgery.

“It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn’t ended,” Soltani told CNN by phone. “I’m worried. I’m hoping it will be good but I’m worried it will get very ugly.”

For millions of Iranian-Americans, the mix of dread, optimism, tension and anger had become part of daily life as they tried to learn whether Iranian authorities would violently suppress demonstrations over the previous week’s election.

President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had been announced as the landslide winner of the vote, which opposition groups said had been falsified. Independent observers were not allowed to monitor the election.

Concerns about possible bloodshed grew after supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a warning statement on Friday. Iranian officials had already disrupted normal lines of communication, including mobile phone service, and had prohibited foreign news organizations from reporting on the protests.

Despite a ban on demonstrations, thousands of people went into the streets on Saturday. Police met them with batons, tear gas and water cannons.

For Yazdi, the instability and lack of information are deeply personal. Her grandfather, a veteran Iranian political figure, was arrested from his hospital bed during the week. He has since been taken back to the hospital, she said, but she does not know whether he may be detained again or what might happen to other family members.

“It’s very exhausting,” Yazdi said. “I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don’t care about the risks involved.”

According to Yazdi, her parents, who left Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, think that kind of thinking is unwise. They share her fears, she said, but believe going back now would be far too dangerous.

“There’s a generation gap, a culture gap,” she said.

That divide, she explained, is central to her identity as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States, someone who still calls Iranians “my people.”

“Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I’m culturally confused,” Yazdi said. “I’m not completely American the right way, and I’m not completely Iranian the right way.”

Soltani also spoke about a divide between generations of Iranian-Americans, though he framed it mainly in political terms. He said his parents’ generation lost everything during the revolution and would only think about returning to Iran if the revolutionary government were removed from power.

Many older Iranian-Americans in the United States “actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you’re just legitimizing the government,” Soltani said. He summarized their view this way: “We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you’re going to the other team.”

“They think the system needs to go completely,” he said. “All they care is for the system to collapse. They think if the system collapses, they’re going to be able to go back.”

Whatever the outcome, both Soltani and Yazdi said the events of the week had permanently altered Iran.

“I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive,” Soltani said. “Even if they fail now, the people know if they get in the streets in millions, they’re not going to be able to stop them.”

Iranian-Americans across the United States anxiously followed the unfolding protests in Iran after the country’s disputed presidential election, relying on television reports, Facebook updates, text messages, online videos, and repeated phone calls to relatives for news. As Iranian authorities restricted communications, blocked websites, disrupted mobile phone service, and barred many foreign journalists from reporting freely, families abroad struggled to understand what was happening on the streets of Tehran and other cities.

For many in the Iranian diaspora, the crisis was deeply personal. Parents tried to reach children, siblings called one another across time zones, and friends searched social-networking sites for signs that loved ones were safe. Each new image of crowds, police, tear gas, or injured protesters brought a mixture of fear and hope. Some Iranian-Americans said they were inspired by the courage of demonstrators challenging the official results, while others worried that the government would answer the protests with overwhelming force.

The unrest followed the government’s announcement that President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had won re-election by a wide margin, a result rejected by supporters of opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi. Demonstrators poured into the streets, alleging fraud and demanding that their votes be counted. The scale of the protests, among the largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, shocked observers and raised urgent questions about the future of Iran’s political system.

In the United States, Iranian-Americans gathered in homes, community centers, and public demonstrations to watch events unfold and show solidarity with protesters. Some wore green, the color associated with Mousavi’s campaign and the opposition movement. Others circulated videos, translated messages from inside Iran, and urged American officials and international organizations to pay attention without giving Iranian authorities a pretext to portray the movement as foreign-backed.

The uncertainty was agonizing. Because official information from Iran was limited and often distrusted, rumors spread quickly. A video posted online or a brief call from Tehran could shift the mood from optimism to panic. Many Iranian-Americans described feeling powerless: close enough to understand the stakes, but too far away to protect relatives or influence events directly.

Their emotions reflected the broader significance of the crisis. The protests were not only a domestic confrontation over an election result; they became a global moment watched intensely by Iranians everywhere. For those living abroad, the demonstrations revived memories of revolution, repression, exile, and hopes for political change. The question hanging over the community was whether the government would compromise with protesters or violently crush a movement demanding accountability.

As the standoff continued, Iranian-Americans remained glued to every available source of information. Their fear, frustration, and hope underscored how far the crisis reached beyond Iran’s borders, binding families and communities abroad to the fate of demonstrators facing danger at home.

counterfactuals.output:
**Communication Blackouts Leave Iranian-American Families Anxious as Tehran Unrest Spreads**

*By Staff Writer*

As post-election unrest gripped Tehran, Iranian-American families across the United States found themselves trapped between breaking news alerts and unanswered phone calls, struggling to reach parents, siblings, cousins, and friends in a city where communication had become uncertain and fear was spreading quickly.

In the days after Iran’s disputed presidential election, protests filled Tehran’s streets and security forces moved to suppress demonstrations. For many Iranian Americans watching from Los Angeles, Washington, New York, and other communities with large Iranian diasporas, the political crisis was deeply personal. Their concern was not only about the outcome of the vote, but about whether loved ones were safe.

Phone calls that once connected easily to Tehran began failing or cutting out. Text messages went unanswered. Internet access slowed or disappeared. Social media posts appeared briefly, then stopped. Families tried landlines, mobile phones, email, messaging apps, and contacts through friends of friends—anything that might produce even a few words of reassurance.

For many, silence became the most frightening signal.

Parents in the U.S. worried about adult children in Tehran who had joined demonstrations or lived near protest routes. Younger Iranian Americans, more connected through online networks, searched for video clips, translated updates, and checked social media feeds late into the night. Older generations often relied on satellite television, Persian-language radio, and repeated calls to relatives, listening for small clues in voices that might reveal danger.

The unrest also exposed generational differences within Iranian-American families. Younger members, especially those born or raised in the United States, often spoke with open hope about change in Iran and saw the protests as a sign of courage and possibility. Many followed the events in real time online and shared news rapidly across digital platforms.

Their parents and grandparents, however, often viewed the crisis through memories of revolution, war, imprisonment, or exile. For them, public protest carried a heavier fear. Some urged relatives in Tehran to stay home, avoid crowds, and speak cautiously on the phone. Even when they sympathized with demonstrators, they worried that hope could be met with violence.

Those differences sometimes led to tense conversations in Iranian-American households. Younger family members wanted to amplify voices from inside Iran; older relatives warned against drawing attention to people still living there. One generation saw a historic opening. Another remembered the cost of being visible.

Communication blackouts deepened that divide. When contact with Tehran was lost, families filled the gaps with worry. A missed call could mean a dead battery, a blocked network, or something worse. A vague message—“We are fine, don’t worry”—could be read as either comfort or a sign that someone was afraid to speak freely.

Despite the fear, many families held onto hope. Each successful phone call, each short email, each message passed through a relative in another city became a moment of relief. Some Iranian Americans described hearing determination in the voices of relatives in Tehran, even when those relatives avoided details. Others said the very act of trying to communicate—calling again and again across distance and disruption—became a form of solidarity.

For the diaspora, the unrest transformed daily life. Families kept televisions on through the night, monitored news sites, and gathered in community centers, homes, and public demonstrations in the United States. Iranian-American students organized vigils. Parents attended rallies with caution and emotion. Green ribbons, candles, and handwritten signs became symbols not only of political protest, but of connection to relatives living under pressure.

The uncertainty was especially painful because so many Iranian Americans had long maintained family bonds across borders through regular communication. A weekly phone call to Tehran, a video chat with grandparents, or a quick exchange of family photos had helped soften the distance created by migration and politics. When those channels faltered, the distance felt suddenly larger.

In many households, fear and hope existed side by side. Families feared arrests, injuries, and reprisals. They feared that relatives’ names, faces, or online comments could bring danger. But they also hoped the protests signaled a new political awakening and that the world was paying attention.

As the unrest continued, Iranian-American families remained suspended between two realities: the safety of their lives in the United States and the vulnerability of loved ones in Tehran. With every failed call and every brief message, they were reminded that political upheaval is not only measured in crowds and headlines, but in the quiet panic of families waiting for someone to answer the phone.

counterfactuals.output:
**Iranian-Americans watch, worry as protests shake Tehran**

*By [Staff Writer], CNN-style news article*

She keeps the television on low, the glow flickering across her apartment long after midnight. Her laptop is open to Facebook, where messages appear in bursts — some in English, some in Persian, some only a few words long: “They are in the streets.” “Basij are coming.” “Pray for us.”

On the table beside her, two phones sit charged and waiting. One is for calls from relatives in Iran. The other is for friends in the United States who, like her, are not sleeping.

For a young Iranian-American woman thousands of miles from Tehran, the nights since Iran’s disputed presidential election have become a blur of cable news, online videos, text messages and fear. She refreshes Web pages again and again, searching for names, faces, any sign that the people she loves are safe.

“I feel like if I sleep, I’ll miss something,” she says. “And what if the next thing I miss is someone getting hurt?”

Across the United States and around the world, members of the Iranian diaspora have been living in two time zones: their bodies in Los Angeles, Washington, New York and Toronto, their attention fixed on Iran, where protests erupted after officials declared President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the overwhelming winner of a second term.

The results, announced soon after polls closed, stunned supporters of opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi, who had drawn massive crowds during a campaign that energized young voters, women and urban Iranians hoping for political change. Many believed the vote count was implausible. Within hours, accusations of fraud spread rapidly, and the color green — Mousavi’s campaign color — became the symbol of a widening opposition movement.

In Tehran, demonstrators poured into the streets by the hundreds of thousands, chanting “Where is my vote?” and calling for a new election. Some marched silently, hands raised in peace. Others held posters of Mousavi or wore green wristbands and headscarves.

The government responded with warnings, arrests and force. Riot police and members of the Basij militia confronted protesters in the capital and other cities. Foreign journalists faced restrictions, making it difficult to independently verify accounts from inside Iran. In the absence of traditional reporting, shaky cell phone videos, Twitter posts, Facebook updates and YouTube clips became central to the world’s view of the unrest.

Images of crowds running from tear gas, young people bloodied in the streets and security forces on motorcycles spread quickly online. For many outside Iran, those fragments were the only connection to a fast-moving crisis.

Iranian authorities defended the election results and accused foreign governments and media organizations of encouraging unrest. Ahmadinejad dismissed the demonstrations, comparing some protesters to disappointed fans after a soccer match. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei later endorsed the outcome and warned that continued demonstrations would not be tolerated.

But the protests continued, fueled by anger over the vote and by broader frustrations with political repression, economic hardship and limits on personal freedom.

For Iranian-Americans watching from afar, the moment has been both inspiring and agonizing. Many say they are proud to see Iranians demanding accountability, but terrified by the risks protesters face.

At rallies in U.S. cities, demonstrators have held green flags and signs reading “We are all Iranians” and “Stop the violence.” Some have marched in silence, echoing the early demonstrations in Tehran. Others have gathered outside Iranian interest offices or public squares, chanting in Persian and English.

Yet even outside Iran, fear remains. Some Iranian-Americans avoid giving full names, worried that speaking publicly could endanger relatives back home. Others say family members in Iran have warned them not to call too often, not to mention politics on the phone, not to assume anyone’s conversations are private.

The uncertainty has made every message feel urgent.

A missed call can trigger panic. A delayed email can feel ominous. A short Facebook update — “I’m OK” — can bring temporary relief.

The young woman in her apartment says she has not seen her relatives in Iran for years. Still, every image from the protests feels personal. The streets on television are streets her parents knew. The chants are in the language spoken at her family’s dinner table. The faces in the crowds look like cousins, neighbors, classmates.

“It’s not just politics,” she says. “It’s people. It’s our families. It’s everyone wondering what kind of future Iran is going to have.”

As the Iranian government tightens control over information, activists continue to rely on social media and underground networks to share news. But the same tools that help broadcast the protests also expose participants to danger. Videos and photographs can identify demonstrators. Online posts can be tracked. Rumors can spread as quickly as facts.

Still, many Iranians have continued to take the risk.

The unrest has become one of the most serious domestic challenges to Iran’s leadership since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Whether it will force political change remains uncertain. The state retains powerful security institutions, and opposition leaders operate under intense pressure.

But the protests have already altered perceptions inside and outside Iran. They have shown deep divisions within the country and revealed a generation willing to confront authority despite the consequences.

For those watching from abroad, the days are measured in updates, the nights in worry.

The young Iranian-American woman finally turns down the television as dawn approaches. Her phones are still beside her. Facebook is still open. In Tehran, another day is beginning.

She knows she should sleep.

Instead, she presses refresh.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a human-interest news story about diaspora reactions to the 2009 Iranian protests, featuring Atefeh Yazdi, whose grandfather Ebrahim Yazdi was arrested, and Reza Soltani describing the anxiety from Houston.
counterfactuals.output:
**Far From Tehran, Iranians in Houston Wait, Worry and Watch**

*By Staff Writer*

HOUSTON — For many Iranians living abroad, the images from Tehran in June 2009 arrived in fragments: shaky cellphone videos, hurried phone calls, text messages cut short, and satellite broadcasts replayed late into the night.

For Atefeh Yazdi, the political crisis unfolding in Iran became painfully personal when she learned that her grandfather, Ebrahim Yazdi, had been arrested amid the government crackdown that followed the disputed presidential election.

Ebrahim Yazdi, a veteran Iranian political figure and former foreign minister, was among the reformist and opposition figures detained as protests spread across Iran after the announced re-election of President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad. Demonstrators accused authorities of manipulating the vote, while the government denounced the unrest and moved quickly to suppress it.

From afar, Atefeh Yazdi joined a diaspora community caught between helplessness and urgency. Like many Iranian Americans, she followed events hour by hour, searching for reliable information while fearing that each new report could bring worse news about relatives, friends or political activists.

Across Houston, home to a large Iranian community, the protests turned private homes, university campuses and community gatherings into spaces of mourning, debate and mobilization. Families who had spent years building lives in the United States found themselves pulled back emotionally into Iran’s streets — to Tehran’s avenues, university gates and neighborhoods where protesters were being beaten, arrested or chased by security forces.

Reza Soltani, watching events from Houston, described the atmosphere among Iranian expatriates as one of constant anxiety. The distance, he said, did not make the fear easier to bear. Instead, it created a different kind of anguish: the inability to know what was happening in real time, the uncertainty over whether relatives were safe, and the frustration of being unable to stand beside those marching in Iran.

Phone calls to Iran were often tense and brief. Some relatives avoided speaking openly, worried that conversations could be monitored. Others warned family members abroad not to call too often. News traveled through social media and informal networks, but rumors and confirmed reports were difficult to separate.

Still, the diaspora responded. In Houston and other cities, Iranians gathered for vigils and demonstrations, many wearing green, the color associated with opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi’s campaign and the broader protest movement that became known as the Green Movement. Some carried signs demanding political prisoners be freed. Others held photographs of Neda Agha-Soltan, the young woman whose death during the protests became an international symbol of the crackdown.

For Atefeh Yazdi, her grandfather’s arrest underscored the risks faced by those inside Iran who challenged the official narrative. For Reza Soltani and others in Houston, the unrest was not an abstract foreign crisis but a daily emotional ordeal — one measured in missed calls, sleepless nights and the dread of seeing a familiar name in the news.

The 2009 protests eventually faded from the streets under pressure from arrests and state force, but for many Iranians abroad, the experience left a lasting imprint. It deepened political engagement among some younger members of the diaspora and revived old fears among those who had lived through earlier waves of repression.

In Houston, as in Los Angeles, Washington, Toronto and cities across Europe, Iranians watched the events with a mixture of pride and grief: pride in the courage of protesters demanding accountability, and grief at the cost borne by those inside the country.

For families like the Yazdis, the crisis was also a reminder that exile and distance offer only partial shelter. Even thousands of miles from Tehran, the knock on a door in Iran could still be felt in a living room in Texas.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a journalistic piece in CNN format about Iranian-Americans watching the Green Movement protests from afar, discussing banned demonstrations, Khamenei’s warning, media restrictions, and the emotional divide between younger and older exiles.
counterfactuals.output:
**Iranian-Americans watch unrest in Iran with hope, fear and a generation gap**

*By [Reporter Name], CNN*

For many Iranian-Americans, the images coming out of Iran in the days after the disputed presidential election were both electrifying and painful: crowds in green wristbands filling Tehran’s streets, chants echoing from rooftops, young protesters facing riot police — and then, increasingly, silence as the government moved to restrict the flow of information.

From Los Angeles to Washington, New York to Northern Virginia, Iranian exiles and their children have been watching the Green Movement protests from afar, refreshing websites, calling relatives and scanning shaky cellphone videos posted online before they disappear.

The demonstrations erupted after President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner of the election, a result his challenger Mir Hossein Mousavi and many supporters said was fraudulent. Iranian authorities denied wrongdoing and moved to contain the unrest, banning unauthorized demonstrations and warning opposition leaders against further street protests.

Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei delivered a stern message during Friday prayers, saying the election result would stand and that political leaders would be held responsible for any violence that followed. His warning deepened fears among Iranians abroad that the state’s response could become more forceful.

At the same time, Iran imposed sweeping media restrictions, limiting foreign journalists’ ability to report, revoking press access in some cases and warning news organizations against covering protests without permission. With professional reporting constrained, social media, text messages and amateur video became lifelines for families overseas trying to understand what was happening.

For younger Iranian-Americans — many born or raised in the United States — the protests have felt like a moment of awakening.

They have gathered at vigils outside federal buildings, on college campuses and in public squares, wearing green ribbons and holding signs that read “Where is my vote?” Some say the movement has connected them to a homeland they know mostly through parents’ stories, family visits and Persian-language satellite television.

“I grew up hearing about Iran as something lost,” said one Iranian-American student at a rally in California. “Now I feel like I’m watching people my age trying to take it back.”

But among older exiles, the emotions are often more complicated.

Many left Iran after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, or during the years of repression and war that followed. They have seen mass mobilization before, and they remember how quickly hope can give way to crackdown. For them, the images of crowds in Tehran evoke both pride and dread.

Some older Iranian-Americans worry that Western attention could endanger protesters by allowing authorities in Tehran to portray the movement as foreign-backed. Others fear that the demonstrators, many of them young and unarmed, are underestimating the state’s willingness to use force.

“They are brave,” said an Iranian exile in the Washington area who left Iran decades ago. “But we know this government. We know what it can do.”

That divide — between the optimism of younger activists and the caution of older exiles — has played out in homes and community centers across the Iranian diaspora. Parents urge restraint; children demand visibility. Older relatives warn against slogans that sound revolutionary; younger demonstrators insist silence would be a betrayal.

Still, across generations, there is a shared sense of anguish at watching events unfold from thousands of miles away.

Phone calls to Iran are brief and guarded. Relatives speak in coded language, aware that conversations may be monitored. Some families say they have been unable to reach loved ones near protest sites. Others wait anxiously for names of the detained or injured.

The restrictions on media have only intensified that uncertainty. In the absence of verified reports, rumors spread quickly — of arrests, beatings, deaths and disappearances. Each new video clip is examined for clues: a street sign, a voice, a date, a face in the crowd.

For Iranian-Americans, the Green Movement has become more than a political crisis abroad. It is a test of memory, identity and belonging. Those who fled Iran see echoes of the past. Their children see a possible future.

And while the demonstrations inside Iran have been banned and warned against by the country’s highest authority, their impact has traveled far beyond Tehran’s streets — into diaspora communities where hope and fear now sit side by side.
